newsitem.headline: Reuters 6th ex-Madrid air cargo market report.

text.p: This is a repeat of Reuters' 6th ex-Madrid air cargo market report. It will be published reguarly until a new version is issued at a later date.

* The tariffs represent average market rates calculated from a range of prices and are indicative of current market activity.
Vegetables boost ex-Madrid air cargo business, rates steady.
By Julia Hayley

MADRID, Jan 21 (Reuter) - Booming exports of fresh vegetables are filling air cargo space from Madrid to North America and compensating for the otherwise slack winter trade, airlines and cargo agents said.
The average price was higher on several North American destinations, but rates are generally holding steady and are not expected to change until April or May, they said.
"It's tomatoes and little else," a U.S. airline cargo salesman said of the January market.
Bad weather in the U.S. had added to demand for fresh vegetables from Europe, another airline official said.
"It's always difficult to boost business in January but there are vegetables in abundance for North Atlantic routes and all our flights are full," said a cargo official at Iberia.
"This usually keeps up until March," he said, adding that he did not expect rates to change in the short term although certain airlines might adjust their prices up or down on specific destinations.

Madrid-New York prices quoted by airlines and general sales agents ranged from 133 pesetas to 220 pesetas a kilo for 100 kilos, but the airline with the highest price said this was usually negotiable, particularly for customers who would offer regular business.
"The reality depends on someone coming along and saying he'll put a fixed amount of kilos of cargo on all our flights and he'll usually get a lower price," an official at the airline said.
Rates fall sharply for larger quantities of cargo. A 1,000 kilo load would fly for around 120 pesetas a kilo, for example.
Demand for space for perishable goods from Madrid is concentrated on New York and to a lesser extent Miami. Some is also going by road to Paris to be loaded onto direct flights to Canada.
Airlines and freight forwarders with few direct flights to North America from Madrid are suffering most from the post Christmas fall in cargo volumes.
"This always happens after Christmas but we are at least seeing good business flying textiles to the Middle East," said a freight forwarder with little North Atlantic perishable business.

A GSA with U.S. airline clients said there was reasonable demand on flights to Miami for goods such as shoes and for general cargo which could then go by charter flight to other destinations in Central or South America.
Demand to Latin America, which has exceded capacity in recent months, was lower overall but steady.
GSA Genair said it was taking a lot of telecommunications equipment to Argentina, Peru and Colombia, countries where Spain's Telefonica is expanding through its local affiliates.

Average cargo rates showed some variation on Middle and Far Eastern routes, but this was mainly because fewer Spanish-based agents quote prices there and the sample is smaller than for transatlantic routes.
Rates are usually revised in October or November and again in April or May.

November's 13 pesetas a kilo fuel surcharge, applied by many airlines, took the place of the autumn rate rise, industry sources said. They suspect that, barring a sudden fall in the world oil price, this will gradually turn into a permanent rate rise.
"People did not want to raise rates directly last year because of the fuel surcharge," Genair said, adding that the natural thing would be to expect a rise in the spring.
Others also said they were bracing for higher prices this spring.

"The fuel surcharge will probably be with us for a long time, but independently of that we think rates are going to rise," a freight forwarder said. -Reuters Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax:5017
